title: Jeremiah 38:7–13
context: The narrator introduces Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, a eunuch in the king’s house; the term may describe a palace official, and its exact sense is not pressed. Hearing that Jeremiah was in the dungeon, Ebedmelech goes to the king at Benjamin’s gate, names the officials’ act as evil, and warns that the prophet will die of hunger. The king orders him to take thirty men and lift Jeremiah out. Ebedmelech gathers rags and worn-out garments, lowers them on cords, and tells Jeremiah how to pad the ropes; Jeremiah is drawn up and stays in the court of the guard. Jeremiah 39:15–18 later records the LORD’s promise to deliver Ebedmelech because he trusted in the LORD; that word is named here, not merged into this scene. Both traditions see Ebedmelech’s courage as shared ground: faithful mercy shown at personal risk.

verses.text: Now when Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, a eunuch, who was in the king’s house, heard that they had put Jeremiah in the dungeon (the king was then sitting in Benjamin’s gate),
verses.arminianNotes: Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, a eunuch in the king’s house, hears what was done to Jeremiah while the king sits at Benjamin’s gate. Arminian readers note that the rescuer is an outsider, a foreigner who acts where Judah’s officials did not.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God raising up help from an unexpected quarter. Both traditions read Ebedmelech’s introduction as significant, and they treat the term eunuch carefully, as it may refer to a court office as well as a physical condition.

verses.text: Ebedmelech went out of the king’s house, and spoke to the king, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Ebedmelech leaves the king’s house and goes to speak to the king. Arminian readers see courage in action: he does not wait for others but takes the risk of approaching the king himself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a man moved to act by concern for God’s prophet, whatever the danger. Shared ground: both traditions read his initiative as faithful mercy, done openly at real personal risk.

verses.text: “My lord the king, these men have done evil in all that they have done to Jeremiah the prophet, whom they have cast into the dungeon. He is likely to die in the place where he is, because of the famine; for there is no more bread in the city.”
verses.arminianNotes: Ebedmelech tells the king the men have done evil to Jeremiah, who will die of famine in the dungeon. Arminian readers note that he names the wrong plainly, refusing to soften it before the king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see bold truth-telling that calls the king to account. Both traditions read the speech as a model of speaking up for the vulnerable, joining moral clarity with respect for the king’s office.

verses.text: Then the king commanded Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, saying, “Take from here thirty men with you, and take up Jeremiah the prophet out of the dungeon, before he dies.”
verses.arminianNotes: The king commands Ebedmelech to take thirty men and lift Jeremiah out before he dies. Arminian readers see the king’s mind changed by an honest appeal, showing that a timely word can turn a decision.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God working through the king’s command to preserve his servant. Shared ground: both traditions read the order as rescue made possible by one person’s courage, and they note the king’s wavering between 38:5 and 38:10.

verses.text: So Ebedmelech took the men with him, and went into the house of the king under the treasury, and took from there rags and worn-out garments, and let them down by cords into the dungeon to Jeremiah.
verses.arminianNotes: Ebedmelech takes rags and worn-out garments from beneath the treasury and lowers them by cords to Jeremiah. Arminian readers see thoughtful compassion that attends to the prophet’s comfort, not merely his rescue.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the humble materials used for so important a deliverance. Both traditions read the detail as showing that mercy pays attention to small things, and they find in it a picture of practical care.

verses.text: Ebedmelech the Ethiopian said to Jeremiah, “Now put these rags and worn-out garments under your armpits under the cords.” Jeremiah did so.
verses.arminianNotes: Ebedmelech tells Jeremiah to put the rags under his armpits beneath the cords, and Jeremiah does so. Arminian readers see gentle care to spare the weakened prophet further injury as he is lifted.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the rescuer’s careful instructions as kindness joined to wisdom. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as tender detail that honors Ebedmelech’s character, and they note Jeremiah’s willing cooperation.

verses.text: So they lifted Jeremiah up with the cords, and took him up out of the dungeon; and Jeremiah remained in the court of the guard.
verses.arminianNotes: They lift Jeremiah from the dungeon with the cords, and he remains in the court of the guard. Arminian readers note that rescue brings relief but not freedom; the prophet is still confined.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s preservation of his servant, sufficient for the work still before him. Both traditions read the verse as deliverance within ongoing hardship, and they name 39:15–18 as the LORD’s later word to Ebedmelech without merging the scenes.
